question: How does a quiet theme become a forceful return?
intro: Chopin gives the piano the title of a narrative poem without supplying a plot. Two themes return in altered proportions, and a fast coda overturns the measured pace of the opening.

sections.label: Lyrical return · approximate
sections.mNote: E♭-major song enlarged into a forceful chordal statement

sections.label: First theme recalled · approximate
sections.mNote: shortened G-minor recollection prepares the coda

cues.title: Before the regular pulse
cues.text: The introduction sets rising octaves against pauses and quieter chords. Listen for the change from a single line spread across the keyboard to melody with accompaniment, rather than expecting the main theme’s pace from the first note.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note describes the octave introduction and its transition to the first theme. The report shows contrasting attacks and quiet spaces in the opening half-minute. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A broad underlying pulse
cues.text: Through the first theme, try grouping the six quarter-note beats into two broad halves. The melody can lean across those groups while the accompaniment maintains their movement.
cues.evidence: The Moderato is notated in 6/4. This is a listening suggestion for the first-theme passage, not a claim that a particular bar begins at this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Keep the singing line
cues.text: As the keyboard writing becomes busier, follow the longer melodic notes rather than giving every attack equal attention. Melody and decoration can move at different rates within one hand’s part.
cues.evidence: Howard describes the alternation of lyricism and passagework. The analysis records changing attack density around 1:45–2:00 but cannot identify the melody independently.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Restraint gives way
cues.text: Across this stretch, the piano gains force and activity. Compare the sound with the quiet first theme: expansion can involve more attacks, a wider register and greater weight without introducing a new tune.
cues.evidence: The report shows a sustained increase in relative level from about 2:05 to 2:40, with more detected attacks around 2:35. Register is offered as a listening comparison, not a measured transcription.

cues.title: Room for another phrase
cues.text: Around this passage, the forceful writing gives way to quieter, more widely spaced attacks. Listen to how that release makes room for a longer-breathed melodic span.
cues.evidence: The largest detected change is near 3:06. Relative level and attack density both fall around 3:10–3:20; the report does not establish an exact theme entrance.

cues.title: Remember the quieter scale
cues.text: Keep the quieter lyrical writing in mind for the later returns. Compare the length of the phrases and the weight of their accompaniment, not just whether you recognise the tune.
cues.evidence: Howard identifies a lyrical second theme that later becomes much more forceful. The cue invites comparison without assigning a precisely aligned statement. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The middle gathers weight
cues.text: Across this central stretch, quiet writing grows into a much stronger passage. Follow the accumulating sound without assuming that every increase in force marks a new formal section.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises strongly between about 4:45 and 5:00, after the detected change near 4:32. The measured contour does not itself identify a thematic transformation.

cues.title: A line inside the weight
cues.text: Through the stronger central passage, try to retain a sense of a long melodic line inside the chords and faster notes. A sustained phrase can remain the organising idea even when its accompaniment gains weight.
cues.evidence: The report shows a sustained high-level stretch around 5:00–5:40. The distinction between melody and surrounding activity is an editorial listening invitation, not an automatic voice separation.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Schumann’s favourite
cues.text: Schumann reported telling Chopin during his 1836 Leipzig visit that the G minor Ballade was his favourite of Chopin’s works. In that account, Chopin replied that he preferred it too. This records an exchange of judgement, not a hidden literary programme.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil programme note quotes Schumann’s account of the conversation. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23

cues.title: Activity is not force
cues.text: In this stretch, compare the number of attacks with the weight of the sound. The piano can become busier while its relative level falls; faster surface movement need not produce a heavier phrase.
cues.evidence: Around 6:25–6:35, the report shows falling relative level alongside more detected attacks. This describes a short contrast within the passage, not a tempo measurement.

cues.title: Compare the returning themes
cues.text: In the later returns, compare familiar melodies with their earlier presentations. Listen for changes in accompaniment and scale: recognising a tune is only the first part of recognising what its return does.
cues.evidence: The work’s recurring themes are described in Howard’s commentary. Their precise return boundaries have not been aligned to this performance. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A quieter preparation
cues.text: Across the passage before the final rush, the sound falls back substantially. Listen to the space this creates between the broad preceding statements and the concentrated activity of the ending.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a sustained reduction around 7:35–8:00 before a rise around 8:05–8:10. It does not establish a particular harmonic preparation.

cues.title: The fast coda
cues.text: The closing section is marked Presto con fuoco. Follow its larger two-beat measures rather than counting every fast note; the change of gait matters as well as the accumulation of attacks.
cues.evidence: The score’s coda is in cut time. Its approximate location follows the work’s closing structure and increased recorded activity after 8:05; it has not been checked by ear.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Accents inside the rush
cues.text: Through the coda, listen for accented notes within the running figures. A rapid surface does not make every note equally important; larger groupings give the ending its direction.
cues.evidence: This is a score-informed listening suggestion for the closing Presto, not an automatically detected accent pattern. The report shows sustained activity around 8:25–9:05.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The rush is interrupted
cues.text: The closing stretch alternates forceful gestures with much quieter gaps. Attend to the waiting as well as the attacks: each renewed gesture has to recover momentum after the preceding withdrawal.
cues.evidence: Relative level alternates sharply around 9:20–9:45, while detected attacks become sparse. Five-second windows support this pattern but not the precise start of a rest.

cues.title: After the final attacks
cues.text: Across the final passage, renewed activity gives way to a long decay. Listen through the remaining resonance rather than treating the last forceful gesture as an instantaneous end.
cues.evidence: A renewed burst appears around 9:50; no further attacks are detected in the 10:05–10:10 windows, and relative level falls sharply. No key claim is taken from the unreliable final estimate.

transitions.title: Declamation finds a regular bass
transitions.how: The Largo begins by outlining A♭ major, the flattened-supertonic harmony of G minor, in bare octaves. Its pauses and final dissonance postpone a settled tonic. The Moderato answers with G-minor melody and a bass-and-chord accompaniment: the keyboard separates into singer and support. The metre changes from 4/4 to 6/4, heard as two broad groups of three. Instead of extending the introduction’s rising declamation, Chopin lets the quieter, circling theme establish the movement’s ordinary pulse.
transitions.evidence: The approximate First theme boundary is 0:30. The report shows sparse, quiet attacks at 0:20–0:30 followed by stable G-minor estimates. The Largo’s A♭-major outline, dissonant ending and change to Moderato in 6/4 come from the score; Orrin Howard describes this textural join at https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23.

transitions.title: The running notes release a song
transitions.how: The first theme’s G-minor world expands into forceful passagework, then loses both weight and attack density before the E♭-major lyrical theme. The new key is G minor’s submediant, not its relative major, B♭. Chopin keeps the broad 6/4 frame but exchanges the agitated surface for a longer upper melody over gently moving broken chords. The bass now supports the phrase rather than driving the keyboard across its registers; the release is part of the arrival.
transitions.evidence: The approximate Lyrical theme boundary is 3:20. The report’s strongest novelty peak is earlier, at 3:06, with a sustained fall in relative level and attacks through 3:20. E♭ major and the change of keyboard texture are score-derived; the span includes the withdrawal rather than asserting an exactly located cadence.

transitions.title: A familiar contour changes harmonic ground
transitions.how: Chopin leaves the E♭-major song by bringing back the first theme in A minor. Recognition comes from its melodic shape and accompanied 6/4 gait, not from recovering G minor. E-major dominant harmony gives this transposed return its new centre; the quiet restatement then gathers weight towards the second theme’s enlarged A-major appearance. The change from C♮ to C♯ eventually turns the new tonic from minor to major while retaining A as its root.
transitions.evidence: The Central transformations boundary is 4:32, a report novelty peak; the quieter 4:30–4:45 stretch is followed by a rise towards 5:00. The score supplies the A-minor first-theme return and subsequent A-major transformation. The report’s E-major estimates are treated as compatible with dominant emphasis, not as a replacement formal key analysis.

transitions.title: The second theme arrives first
transitions.how: The central passagework opens into the lyrical theme in E♭ major, now weighted with full chords and a much more forceful accompaniment. Chopin restores its original key but not its earlier scale of utterance. The bass supports a broad, chordal proclamation where the first statement had offered a lightly accompanied song. This return comes before the first theme: the order of the opening themes is reversed, so the apparent arrival still leaves G minor to be recovered.
transitions.evidence: The Lyrical return section is provisionally placed at 7:00. The report shows sustained stronger playing around 6:40–7:20, rather than a unique onset at 7:00. The score establishes the E♭-major chordal return and reversed thematic order; the relations file explicitly notes these returns but publishes no fixed-lag match.

transitions.title: Major-key weight gives way to minor
transitions.how: The E♭-major proclamation subsides into the first theme in G minor. The keys share G and B♭; restoring D in place of E♭ changes the harmonic centre without requiring an unrelated melodic idea. Chopin strips away the second theme’s chordal weight and recovers the first theme’s quieter contour. This is a shortened recollection, not a restart: its continuation directs attention towards D-major dominant harmony and the coming coda.
transitions.evidence: The First theme recalled boundary at 7:34 matches a novelty peak. Relative level falls across 7:20–7:45; the score supplies the E♭-major to G-minor return and its subsequent dominant preparation. Shared triad notes explain the tonal relationship, not a claimed single pivot chord.

transitions.title: The dominant releases a different gait
transitions.how: The recalled theme narrows towards D-major dominant harmony, leaving G minor as an unfulfilled destination. Presto con fuoco releases that pressure into a new cut-time coda. The former 6/4 sway is replaced by two urgent beats, with displaced accents and running figures distributed across the keyboard. Chopin does not simply play the old melody faster: the bass, chord attacks and rapid upper writing establish a new texture that drives towards the final G-minor closure.
transitions.evidence: The Fast coda boundary at 8:06 coincides with a novelty peak and the rise in relative level from 8:00 to 8:10. The score supplies the dominant preparation, Presto con fuoco and cut-time change. The preceding quiet span is included because its duration is part of the join; no bar is aligned to the timestamp.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
